assessmentSummary.identity: A straight-elbow isometric suspension from a secure bar or stable rings with an intentionally active scapular position, usually described as drawing the shoulders slightly away from the ears. The position must remain small, controlled, comfortable, and explicitly distinct from both a passive Dead Hang and repeated Scapular Pull-Ups.
currentCardFindings: Active Hang Scapular Hold and Active Dead Hang are exact historical aliases or duplicate sources, not separate exercises.
The active card now retains legacy sources 820, 857, and 1074 and archives the redundant source variants without making them selectable.
The historical Dead Hang / Active Hang card was split because its two scapular modes cannot share one selectable variant.
The cue is active scapular engagement with straight elbows, not a maximal forced down-and-back position and not the first repetition of a pull-up.
Physical difficulty exceeds exercise complexity because the grip and actively engaged shoulder girdle support relative bodyweight.
Exercise difficulty is assessed from complexity and physical demand. Audience experience remains workout context and is not stored as an exercise-card level.
Five media links are candidate discoveries only. No exact-match decision, safety review, caption review, reviewer identity, or approval has been recorded.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: straight-arm isometric is simple to sequence but requires full relative grip load plus active scapular force
stable foot support meaningfully unloads the grip and shoulder girdle without changing the active scapular solution
band assistance reduces load but adds band entry, recoil, and exit management
freely rotating rings increase stabilization and grip-orientation demand without changing the isometric movement solution
added load increases grip and active scapular isometric demand and adds load-attachment and controlled-exit requirements
one arm bears the suspension load while asymmetric shoulder and trunk control and exit demands rise

proposedLoadProfile.recoveryHours: dose_and_context_dependent; count total active-hang time with pull-ups, climbing, carries, rope work, rings, and other grip or scapular-depression loading

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the athlete repeatedly finds the same active position without elbow flexion pain swing or grip loss; reduce assistance or add modest time before adding load

coachCues: Check the anchor and step-down first
Move the shoulders slightly away from the ears
Hold the small active position without forcing the shoulder blades together
Keep the ribs and body quiet
Step down before the shoulders drift or the grip opens
athleteInstructions: Pull your shoulders a little away from your ears
Hold that position without bending your elbows or swinging
Step down while you can still hold the same shape

programmingDecision.fatigueBudget: count time and assistance-adjusted exposure toward grip, forearm, scapular-depressor, shoulder, and vertical-pull budgets
programmingDecision.logistics: include bar allocation, assistance setup, finding the active position, hold, dismount, and turnover in duration
programmingDecision.substitutionRule: use foot-assisted Active Hang or a supported straight-arm scapular-depression isometric for the same intent; Dead Hang and Scapular Pull-Up change the assigned action

athleteSupport.plainLanguagePrompt: Straight arms, shoulders a little away from your ears, stay still, breathe, and step down before the shape changes.
athleteSupport.feedbackPrompt: Could you keep the same active shoulder position without bending your elbows or losing your grip?

limitations: No direct trial was located that establishes one ideal Active Hang position or dose across populations.
Pull-up kinematics research is adjacent and does not directly measure a static Active Hang.
Grip-training studies in climbers do not validate general bar-hang dosing.
Professional instructions use simplified shoulder cues that require individual range and symptom tolerance.
No candidate media has completed exact-match, full-content, cue-quality, accessibility, or human approval review.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Hang from a secure bar or stable rings with straight elbows while actively drawing the shoulders slightly away from the ears, maintaining a controlled trunk position, and stopping before grip or shoulder position changes.

population.clinicalBoundary: Symptoms, instability, recent surgery, neurologic signs, or rehabilitation restrictions require individualized clinician guidance; this card is not rehabilitation instruction.
population.selectionBoundary: Assistance, dose, supervision, and difficulty caps follow current readiness and workout context, never an exercise-card skill level.

fatigueProfile.cumulativeLoadWarning: Count with pull-ups, climbing, carries, rings, rope, and other grip or scapular work.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Exercise selection requires qualified instruction, appropriate progression, safe equipment and space, and individual physical and psychosocial readiness.

Before Active Hang, verify the bar, rings, rack, anchor, clearance, assistance, landing surface, and step-down. Stop for pain or pinching; instability; numbness or tingling; dizziness; a slipping grip; uncontrolled swinging; elbow-position loss; repeated shoulder-position loss; breath distress; or an unsafe dismount.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Training should be individualized and progressed from current readiness and movement competence rather than from a level assigned to an exercise.

Scale Active Hang with a lower bar, stable foot contact, a box, an appropriate assistance band, shorter submaximal efforts, longer rest, plain-language cues, a visible stop signal, and direct supervision. Record exercise complexity and physical difficulty; do not label the exercise card beginner, intermediate, advanced, or elite.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The supplied videos are discovery candidates only. Public title and channel metadata were observed, but availability, embed response, exact exercise and variant match, full sequence, cue quality, safety, captions, accessibility, reviewer identity, and approval remain pending until the separate verification step and human review.

evidence.sourceTitle: Is Hanging from a Bar Worth Your Time? A CrossFit Reality Check
claims: The professional instruction defines an active hanging position by keeping the shoulders engaged and slightly away from the ears.
Treat straight-elbow scapular engagement held without visible repetitions as Active Hang. Hold duration, breathing, trunk shape, assistance, and grip are controlled delivery or variant dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Is Hanging from a Bar Worth Your Time? A CrossFit Reality Check
claims: The source explicitly distinguishes active-shoulder and passive-hang approaches by goal and shoulder position.

Classify Active Hang by active isometric scapular mode, straight elbows, implement, grip, assistance, trunk shape, time, and added load. Do not merge it with passive hanging or dynamic scapular repetitions.
The anatomy reference identifies the lower trapezius with scapular depression and distinguishes depression from elevation, retraction, protraction, and rotation.

Represent scapular depression as the primary active action, with grip, straight-elbow position, the rotator cuff and other scapular stabilizers, and trunk control also modeled. Do not reduce the shoulder complex to one muscle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Scapula kinematics of pull-up techniques: Avoiding impingement risk with training changes
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
claims: Elevated-arm pulling techniques produced different scapulothoracic and glenohumeral kinematics, showing that grip and technique affect shoulder motion.

This adjacent pull-up evidence supports an explicitly defined, comfortable active position and cautions against treating one forced down-and-back cue as universal. It does not directly validate static Active Hang mechanics or safety.

evidence.sourceTitle: Is Hanging from a Bar Worth Your Time? A CrossFit Reality Check
claims: Active hanging requires continued shoulder-girdle engagement instead of allowing the shoulders to remain passive.

Score exercise complexity separately from relative physical difficulty and derive overall as their maximum. Active scapular force raises physical demand above Dead Hang, while coordination, supervision, grip fatigue, and failure consequence remain separate planning dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Comparison of the Effects of Three Hangboard Strength and Endurance Training Programs on Grip Endurance in Sport Climbers
claims: Hanging dose and grip fatigue change with assistance or added load, hold duration, repetition pattern, grip surface, and rest.

For Active Hang, also record scapular-position drift and elbow bend. Count the exposure with pulling, climbing, carries, rings, rope, and other grip or scapular-depression work rather than treating a short static exercise as fatigue-free.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Safe exercise requires appropriate equipment, instruction, supervision, and progression matched to individual readiness.

Require a rated anchor, safe bar height, secure grip, pain-free overhead position, the ability to find a small active scapular position with straight elbows, and a controlled exit. Use foot or band assistance before position quality fails.

evidence.sourceTitle: Train for the Open With CrossFit Affiliate Programming: Pull-Up
claims: The professional pull-up plan uses repeated timed Active Hang sets as a specific pulling-capacity exposure.

That plan demonstrates that sets, hold time, and recovery must be explicit; it is not a universal dose. Begin with shorter assisted holds, preserve position reserve, and progress only after repeatable straight-elbow control.

evidence.sourceTitle: Is Hanging from a Bar Worth Your Time? A CrossFit Reality Check
claims: The professional source cues active hanging by drawing the shoulders slightly away from the ears while staying engaged.

Instructions for Active Hang must include secure grip, straight elbows, small active scapular position, assigned trunk shape, hold endpoint, breathing, and controlled step-down. Avoid maximal depression or aggressive forced retraction.

evidence.sourceTitle: Train for the Open With CrossFit Affiliate Programming: Pull-Up
claims: The plan uses Active Hang as a pulling prerequisite or accessory exposure and separates it from dynamic pull-up technique work.
Use Active Hang when active straight-arm position ownership is the session goal, keep enough reserve for later high-consequence bar tasks, and count cumulative grip and shoulder loading.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Training should reflect individual readiness, competence, and progressive development.

Athlete support should visually compare passive and active positions, show straight elbows, assistance, hold time, safe step-down, and pain, tingling, grip-slip, or shoulder-drift stop signals without assigning a level to the card.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Qualified instruction, safe equipment, supervision, and gradual progression are central to resistance training.

Coach support should include anchor and clearance checks, passive-versus-active mode confirmation, front or side observation, grip and scapular-drift logging, fatigue-order warnings, assistance options, and safe station turnover.

evidence.sourceTitle: Is Hanging from a Bar Worth Your Time? A CrossFit Reality Check
claims: Active and passive positions are intentionally distinguished, while grip, equipment, and loading can be manipulated.
Foot or band assistance, rings, trunk shape, hold time, and added load can be variants or delivery annotations. Dead Hang, Scapular Pull-Up, pull-up, and flexed-arm hang remain separate definitions.

alternateAssessments.name: Foot-Assisted Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Stable foot contact unloads grip and shoulder demand while preserving the straight-elbow active scapular isometric.

alternateAssessments.name: Band-Assisted Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Band assistance reduces relative load but adds entry, recoil, and exit constraints.

alternateAssessments.name: Ring Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Rings preserve active isometric mode while changing grip orientation and stability demand.

alternateAssessments.name: Hollow-Body Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared hollow trunk shape changes body-line emphasis without changing the active straight-arm hang identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Arched Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared arch changes trunk and shoulder orientation but remains an Active Hang only while elbows and scapular position stay isometric.

alternateAssessments.name: Weighted Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Added load materially changes physical difficulty, attachment, dose, recovery, and exit requirements.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Arm Active Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: One-arm active suspension changes laterality, load per limb, asymmetric shoulder and trunk control, and failure consequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Dead Hang
alternateAssessments.rationale: Passive scapular mode removes the active isometric action and changes intent, cues, difficulty, fatigue, and shoulder-position tolerance.

alternateAssessments.name: Scapular Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Repeated scapular motion and controlled return create a dynamic exercise rather than an isometric hold.

alternateAssessments.name: Pull-Up
alternateAssessments.rationale: Elbow flexion and large body displacement add a full vertical-pull action and substantially greater movement and fatigue demands.

alternateAssessments.name: Straight-Arm Support Hold
alternateAssessments.rationale: Supporting the body above bars or rings reverses the force direction and changes shoulder, elbow, grip, and equipment demands.
